author: Caroline Yaffa
title: Public, experts share testimony about controversial SC abortion bill - NewsBreak
text:
By Caroline Yaffa ,
6 hours ago
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WSPA) – A South Carolina Senate subcommittee met Wednesday to hear testimony on Senate Bill 323 , officially titled the Unborn Child Protection Act, which seeks to overhaul the state’s abortion laws by banning nearly all abortions except in cases of medical emergencies.
Introduced in January, the bill would redefine terms like “abortifacient,” “contraception,” and “human embryo,” while removing or changing existing definitions such as “fatal fetal anomaly” and “gestational sac.” It would also eliminate current legal exceptions that allow abortion in cases of rape or incest. The proposed law, if passed as is, would also increase the documentation required of physicians and introduce the risk of civil lawsuits or criminal charges for noncompliance.
Hundreds of people from across South Carolina filled the Statehouse to testify both for and against the bill, with emotions running high during the meeting.
One opponent of the bill, Cora Webb, was removed after an outburst targeting three senators, who are the bill’s sponsors, accusing them of putting lives at risk. On the other side, supporters of the bill made passionate appeals to lawmakers.
Heather Shore, who supports the bill, said, “Roe v. Wade is gone. The responsibility now rests on you… Defend life.”
Tammy Kale added, “No more murders. No more murder of our young. Save our future.”
Under current South Carolina law, abortions are banned after the detection of a fetal heartbeat, which is around six weeks. Governor Henry McMaster expressed his support for the current law, calling.
“I think the way we have settled through all of this work over the years is a good place to settle,” he said.
State Senate Minority Leader Brad Hutto (D – Orangeburg) said he hopes the Governor does what he said he would do.
However, not all Republicans are on board. Two former GOP state senators, Katrina Shealy and Penry Gustafson, delivered emotional testimony against the bill. Both women lost re-election bids after opposing similar legislation.
“You were elected to do what is right, not what will get you reelected,” Shealy told the committee. Gustafson added, “I know how deals are made every year to trade support for this bill or that… there is a lot beyond politics, and it is beautiful to going along to get along staying under the radar, making sure that some GOP group doesn’t target you.”
There were no women present on the Subcommittee, which Gustafson emphasized saying, “where are the women on this committee?”
The subcommittee’s decision could determine whether the bill advances to the Full Committee or stays in the Senate.
